messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Bus Driver
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 53

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Avoid Crowds: Crowded places such as shopping centres or public events
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 21-year-old bus driver, single, living alone in a small apartment in a midwestern city. He came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who noticed he had been calling in sick more often than not, and that his driving had become erratic—jerky stops, sudden lane changes, a constant scanning of the rearview mirror as if he were being followed. What Ethan told his supervisor was that he was tired. What he did not say was that he had not slept more than three hours a night in months, and that when he did sleep, he woke up with his heart pounding, certain he had heard something explode.

The traumatic event had happened two years ago, during his deployment in Afghanistan. Ethan had been a vehicle operator in a logistics convoy. One afternoon, a roadside bomb detonated directly behind his truck. The blast wave threw his vehicle into a ditch. He was not physically injured, but for several minutes after the explosion, he sat in the driver’s seat, unable to move, while the air filled with the smell of burning fuel and something else—something metallic and sweet that he later learned was the smell of a colleague’s body. He did not see the body, but he smelled it. That smell had never left him. It came back in the grocery store when someone walked past with a bag of charcoal briquettes, or when he passed a fast-food restaurant and caught a whiff of burnt grease. Each time, his mouth went dry, his hands locked on the steering wheel, and he had to pull over.

The memory of the event did not come to him as a story he could tell. It came in pieces—a flash of the blast’s orange light, the sound of metal tearing, the sudden silence afterward. He knew what had happened, but when he tried to describe it to a friend from his unit, the words would not come. He would open his mouth and nothing would arrive. The memory played in his mind like a film he could not stop, but it was a film without a plot, only a series of disconnected images that repeated over and over, each time leaving him more exhausted.

He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous. Not just Afghanistan, but everywhere. He had to be on guard all the time. When he drove his bus, he scanned every parked car for a bomb, every pedestrian for a suicide vest. He watched for discarded backpacks, for anyone who looked too tense. He had started avoiding crowds entirely—shopping centres, public events, even the supermarket at peak hours. He had also stopped going to church, which had once been a comfort to him. The silence of the sanctuary felt too close to the silence after the blast, and the smell of incense reminded him of the burnt-sweet smell he could not escape.

To keep the memories at bay, Ethan spent nearly all his time at home on his phone or gaming console. He would play first-person shooters for eight hours straight, the gunfire and explosions on the screen drowning out the sounds in his head. He knew it was not healthy, but it was the only thing that worked. When he turned off the console, the silence returned, and with it the film.

He had come to feel that his life was not worth living anymore. He did not have a plan, but he had stopped caring about things he used to care about—his uniform, his apartment, the small garden he had tried to keep on his balcony. He had stopped returning calls from his mother. He had stopped going to the gym. He had stopped hoping.

What finally brought him to therapy was not the sleeplessness or the avoidance or the despair. It was the morning he was driving his route and a helicopter flew overhead. He slammed on the brakes, threw the bus into park, and sat there shaking, unable to move, while the passengers shouted at him. He knew he could not keep doing this. He was afraid that he would lose his job, and that losing his job would mean losing the only structure he had left. He was also afraid of what he might do if he lost that structure. He did not say that aloud. But when the therapist asked what he hoped to get from therapy, he said, very quietly, “I want to be able to sleep. And I want the film to stop.”
